title: Acid rain
wiki_lead:
Acid rain is rain or any other form of precipitation that is unusually acidic, meaning that it has elevated levels of hydrogen ions (low pH). Most water, including drinking water, has a neutral pH that exists between 6.5 and 8.5, but acid rain has a pH level lower than this and ranges from 4–5 on average. The more acidic the acid rain is, the lower its pH is. Acid rain can have harmful effects on plants, aquatic animals, and infrastructure. Acid rain is caused by emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, which react with the water molecules in the atmosphere to produce sulfuric and nitric acids.
Acid rain has been shown to have adverse impacts on forests, freshwaters, soils, microbes, insects and aquatic life-forms. In ecosystems, persistent acid rain negatively affects tree bark, leaving trees more susceptible to environmental stressors such as drought, fire, solar radiation, frost and pest infestation. Acid rain is also capable of detrimenting soil composition by stripping it of nutrients such as calcium and magnesium which play a critical role in plant growth and maintaining healthy soil. In terms of human infrastructure, acid rain also causes the peeling of paint, corrosion of steel structures, and weathering of stone buildings and statues as well as having impacts on human health.
Some governments, including those in Europe and North America, have made efforts since the 1970s to reduce the release of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide into the atmosphere through air pollution regulations such as the US Clean Air Act and the EU Ambient Air Quality Directive. These efforts have had positive results due to the widespread research on acid rain starting in the 1960s and the publicized information on its harmful effects. The main source of sulfur and nitrogen compounds that result in acid rain are anthropogenic, but nitrogen oxides can also be produced naturally by lightning strikes and sulfur dioxide is produced by volcanic eruptions.

Definition
Acid rain is rain with a pH less than 5. "Clean" or unpolluted rain has a pH greater than 5 but still less than 7 owing to the acidity caused by carbonic acid (H2CO3) according to the following reactions:

H2O + CO2  ⇌  H2CO3
H2O  + H2CO3  ⇌  HCO−3 + H3O+
A variety of natural and human-made sources contribute to the acidity of precipitations. For example nitric acid is produced by electric discharges in the atmosphere such as in lightnings. The usual anthropogenic sources of acid deposition are sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide. They react with water (as does carbon dioxide) to give solutions with pH < 5. Occasional pH readings in rain and fog water of well below 2.4 have been reported in industrialized areas.


History
Acid rain was first systematically studied in Europe in the 1960s, in the United States and Canada in 1970s, and in India in the late 1980s.


In Europe
The corrosive effect of polluted, acidic air of London on limestone and marble was noted in the 17th century by John Evelyn, who remarked upon the poor condition of the Arundel marbles.
Since the Industrial Revolution, emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into the atmosphere have increased. In 1852, Robert Angus Smith was the first to show the relationship between acid rain and atmospheric pollution in Manchester, England. Smith coined the term "acid rain" in 1872.
As soon as the 1960s, European scientists began widely observing and studying the phenomenon. In 1955 two Swedish scientists had already quoted that "the precipitation over Sweden as a whole is definitely more acid than the CO2 equilibrium alone would permit". At first, the main focus in this research laid on local effects of acid rain. Waldemar Christofer Brøgger was the first to acknowledge long-distance transportation of pollutants crossing borders from the United Kingdom to Norway. grok_lead: Acid rain denotes any form of precipitationârain, snow, fog, or hailâexhibiting elevated acidity, typically with a pH below 5.6, in contrast to unpolluted rainfall's natural pH of approximately 5.6 due to dissolved carbon dioxide forming weak carbonic acid. This heightened acidity arises primarily from sulfur dioxide (SO 2) and nitrogen oxides (NO x) emitted by fossil fuel combustion in power plants, industrial processes, and vehicles; these gases undergo oxidation in the atmosphere to yield sulfuric and nitric acids, which then deposit via precipitation or dry fallout, often traveling hundreds of miles from emission sources. The phenomenon gained systematic recognition in the mid-20th century through empirical measurements, notably by ecologist Gene Likens and colleagues at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire, where 1960s data revealed precipitation acidity orders of magnitude exceeding expectations, linking it causally to regional anthropogenic emissions via isotopic tracing of sulfur sources. Environmentally, acid rain accelerates soil and water acidification, mobilizing toxic aluminum that impairs root growth in forests and gill function in fish, contributing to biodiversity losses in oligotrophic lakes and streams, as documented in long-term monitoring of affected regions like the U.S. Northeast and Scandinavian watersheds; it also corrodes limestone structures and metals, though ecosystems in calcareous soils exhibit greater resilience. Regulatory interventions, exemplified by the U.S. Acid Rain Program under the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, imposed emission caps and tradable allowances, yielding over 90% reductions in SO 2 from power plants by deploying scrubbers and low-sulfur fuels, alongside NO x cuts via combustion modifications, which empirical deposition records confirm have reversed acidification trends and fostered aquatic recovery in previously impacted areas. While natural contributors like volcanic eruptions exist, isotopic and emission inventory analyses affirm anthropogenic dominance in industrialized locales, underscoring the efficacy of targeted pollution controls over unsubstantiated broader narratives of irreversible doom.
